children: By Staff Writer

A two-day strike by airport workers has left Kenyan airlines counting heavy losses, disrupted thousands of passengers and freight customers, and sharpened concerns over whether Nairobi can protect its status as a regional aviation hub while Jomo Kenyatta International Airport struggles with congestion and delayed expansion.
And experts say the real economic impact will be felt far beyond airlines and airports and could linger for months.

Kenya Airways, the national flag carrier, said it lost up to $7 million during the two-day go-slow at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, its hub, but acknowledged that the figure did not fully capture the disruption suffered by its customers.“We recognise that the greatest impact was felt by our customers. Many experienced disrupted travel plans, additional expenses and, in some cases, missed personal, business, and commercial opportunities,” said KQ’s board chairman Kiprono Kittony.

Other major airlines in the country, including leading domestic operator Jambojet, Safarilink, and Renegade Air also reported significant disruptions to their operations, leading to flight backlogs that took at least an additional day to clear. Jambojet told The EastAfrican that it cancelled at 60 flights and lost $540,749 in revenues during the two days.

But beyond lost revenues and missed opportunities for airlines and their customers, the strike’s impact was felt far deeper in the Kenyan economy, and experts argue it will continue to impact the country’s aviation and tourism sectors, amid increasing competition for international travellers from neighbouring countries.

The strike came as the Kenya Airports Authority admitted the Jomo Kenyatta International Airport is operating beyond its intended capacity and risks losing market share to new mega airports such as Ethiopia's Bishoftu Airport and Rwanda's Bugesera International Airport unless expansion plans are fast-tracked.

The Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA) is currently handling more passengers than it was designed to and plans to upgrade it are still pending as the State scrambles to obtain financing to move it forward.“There’s a threat of losing market share due to delayed expansion or modernization, especially in light of the rapid development of regional competitors such as Bole lnternational Airport (Addis Ababa), New Kigali lnternational Airport, Bugesera lnternational Airport, Dodoma Msalato lnternational Airport, and Mega Airport City in Bishoftu, Ethiopia,” said the KAA in a recently published disclosure.

With at least 8.9 million passengers travelling though JKIA in 2025, it has been operating far beyond the 7.5 million passengers it was designed to handle every year, exposing passengers to long queues, and degraded facilities such as toilets and waiting bays.

Currently, JKIA is the region’s second busiest airport by passenger traffic, after Addis Ababa’s Bole International Airport which processes roughly 25 million passengers every year, far above the 19 million it was designed to process.
At full completion, the Bishoftu Airport, which will serve as the new hub for Ethiopian Airlines, will serve up to 110 million passengers every year, making it Africa’s largest airport.

The $12.5 billion greenfield project is expected to be fully completed by 2030, capturing more than 10 times JKIA’s capacity and threatening to divert a significant share of international transit traffic from Nairobi.
Competition is also rising from the Bugesera International Airport in Rwanda, whose completion is already ongoing and expected to end by the end of 2028, and begin operations by mid-2029.

When fully completed, it will handle up to 14 million passengers every year, raising Rwanda’s international transit traffic capacity and increasing the current capacity of the Kigali International Airport by up to seven times from the current 2 million.

Traffic diversionTanzania’s Dodoma Msalato Airport also threatens to divert significant traffic from Nairobi. The construction of the airport is almost done, and is set to begin operations soon, becoming the country’s second largest with a capacity of up to 1.75 million passengers per year.

Together with the Julius Nyerere International Airport, which handles up to nine million passengers every year, Msalato airport will eclipse JKIA’s current capacity, risking diversion of some of the traffic.

The upgrade and modernisation of JKIA seek to improve its capacity from the current 7.5 million to 25 million passengers a year, with the construction of a second terminal with new and modern equipment and facilities.
Although the tender has been awarded to Chinese State-owned contractor China Road and Bridge Corporation (CRBC), construction is yet to begin as the State is yet to raise the required funds.

In a recent interview with The EastAfrican, Kenya’s Roads and Transport Cabinet Secretary Davies Chirchir said the government is in advanced stages of getting a syndicated loan arranged by the Trade and Development Bank (TDB) and the African Finance Corporation (AFC).

The borrowed amount, roughly $630 million, will account for 70 percent of the required $900 million for the airport upgrade, with the remaining 30 percent coming from KAA’s Air Passenger Service Charge (APSC) collections.“We’re basically leveraging the Air Passenger Service Charge tax, to basically sell a portion to raise the 30 percent, and we’ll go the market with a bankable project to raise 70 percent,” said Mr Chirchir.

The immediate challenge will be to ensure exporters disruptions won’t happen again. Fresh produce exporters, for instance, lost at least $3 million on each day of the go slow as cargo and freight operations out of key airports were disrupted, leaving flowers, fruits, and vegetable exporters unable to send out their produce.

JKIA alone handles roughly 7,000 tonnes of cargo daily, most of which is fresh produce exports from Kenyan farms. With operations shut, exporters and shippers had to incur extra costs in cold storage, which they say ranged between $0.10 to $0.20 per kilogramme.

But beyond the financially quantifiable losses, analysts argue the damage to the country’s reputation as an aviation hub and tourist destination could be much worse and unquantifiable in monetary terms.“Imagine saving for your dream vacation in Kenya and then end up being stuck at the airport because of a strike. You would write off Kenya completely. How many visitors may have written off the country during the last three strikes?” posed Mohammed Hersi, group director of operations at Pollmans Tours and Safaris, and former chairman of the Kenya Association of Hotelkeepers and Caterers.

He argues that as neighbouring countries build their own reputation as a dream tourist destination, Kenya cannot afford continuous disruptions due to aviation worker strikes, which are completely avoidable.“One strike is forgivable, two may be understandable, but three strikes in under eight months point to serious governance issues. These strikes are avoidable and they come with serious unquantifiable damage, added to the lost revenues for key stakeholders,” he argued.

Sean Mendis, an aviation commentator and former chief operations officer at Accra-based Africa World Airlines, contends that the strikes will long affect Kenya’s reputation as an international transit hub, and with it, the market for Kenya Airways.“Those in Kenya have less choice for the most part, but those of us outside Kenya will simply choose not to include Nairobi in our plans if there is a choice of alternative connecting flights via Addis Ababa or Johannesburg or Dar es Salaam instead,” he told The EastAfrican.

KQ especially, which is banking on increased traffic flow into Kenya for transit to major destinations in US and Europe for growth, stands to lose the most especially because it has already faced reliability challenges due to capacity constraints.

The strike experienced this week was the third major industrial action by Kenya Aviation Workers Union (Kawu) this year, following a strike at JKIA in February and another that was suspended in July after the union and the government reached a framework agreement to address workers’ grievances.
The latest strike came after Kawu said the commitments made in the July agreement had not been adequately implemented.

KAWU had cited unresolved labour issues, including a stalled CBA, disputes over union agency fees, and its recognition dispute with Jambojet. The union also raised concerns over workers’ welfare and employment conditions.

The strike affected JKIA and Wilson Airport in Nairobi, Moi International Airport in Mombasa, Eldoret International Airport and Kisumu International Airport. The disruption was particularly severe at JKIA, which serves as Kenya’s main international aviation hub, with over half of all aircraft movements in the country.

title: ZAWYA: JKIA strike jolts Kenya’s aviation hub ambitions as airlines count losses
